```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(scales)
library(sdotools) # theme_sdo() and the SDO colour scales

# Signed labels read better than a bare minus sign on a diverging chart.
lbl_signed <- function(x) {
  paste0(dplyr::if_else(x >= 0, "+", "−"), scales::comma(abs(round(x))))
}

# Signed number for inline text, with a chosen number of decimals.
fmt_signed <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  paste0(
    dplyr::if_else(x >= 0, "+", "−"),
    scales::comma(abs(x), accuracy = 10^-digits)
  )
}

source_caption <- stringr::str_wrap(
  paste(
    "Source: SDO county single-year-of-age estimates and components of change;",
    "deaths by age estimated from CDPHE public statistics."
  ),
  110
)

# Every published figure: period x grouping x area x sex x age group.
comparison <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("output", "netmig-comparison.csv"),
  col_types = readr::cols(countyfips = "c", caveat = "c")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(sex_label == "Total")

five <- comparison |>
  dplyr::filter(grouping == "five") |>
  dplyr::mutate(age_group = forcats::fct_reorder(age_group, age_order))

broad <- comparison |>
  dplyr::filter(grouping == "broad") |>
  dplyr::mutate(age_group = forcats::fct_reorder(age_group, age_order))

# One value from the five-year table, for inline text.
v5 <- function(county_name, period_name, group, col = "netmig") {
  five |>
    dplyr::filter(
      county == county_name,
      period == period_name,
      age_group == group
    ) |>
    dplyr::pull(.data[[col]])
}

state_now <- five |> dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000", period == "2020-2025")
counties_now <- five |> dplyr::filter(countyfips != "08000", period == "2020-2025")

county_totals <- counties_now |>
  dplyr::summarise(netmig = sum(netmig), .by = county)

total_of <- function(county_name) {
  county_totals |> dplyr::filter(county == county_name) |> dplyr::pull(netmig)
}

validation <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "modelled-deaths-validation.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## What this estimates

The Census Bureau and the State Demography Office publish county population by
age and county net migration in total, but not **net migration by age**. This
analysis recovers it as a demographic residual: for a group of people followed
through time, net migration is what remains of their population change once
births and deaths are taken out.

$$
\text{NM} = \text{Pop}_\text{end} - \text{Pop}_\text{start} - \text{Births} + \text{Deaths}
$$

The residual is formed **one estimate year at a time, by single year of age**,
for every county and sex from July 1990 to July 2025. A one-year cohort is the
group of people of one age on July 1 of one year, followed to July 1 of the
next. Adding up the one-year results for the same people gives exactly their
net migration over a longer period, because the intermediate populations cancel.
Every period, age grouping and custom span in this project is formed that way.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the age labels
Age groups are **age at the end of the period**. "25–29" in 2020–2025 means the
people who were 25–29 on July 1, 2025, who were 20–24 five years earlier.
Children born during a period appear in the youngest groups at its end. Two
groupings are used: eighteen five-year groups (0–4 to 85+) and five broad
groups (0–17, 18–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+).
:::

### Where the numbers come from

| Input | Source |
|---|---|
| Population by single year of age and sex, 1990–2025 | SDO county estimates, ages 0 to 90-and-over (SDO public lookups service) |
| County births, deaths and net migration by year | SDO components of change (SDO public lookups service) |
| Colorado death rates by sex and single year of age | NCHS life tables for Colorado, 1999–2001 and 2018–2023 |
| Each county's age pattern of deaths | CDPHE public 2025 county summary reports, Table 11 |

The SDO single-year estimates top out at an open 90-and-over group before 2010,
so 90+ is the top age in every year.

### Why deaths are estimated, and how

County deaths by age are confidential. Population by age is public, so net
migration by age published from recorded deaths would let anyone work those
deaths back out: deaths = net migration − population change + births. County
deaths by age are therefore **estimated from public data**:

1. Colorado death rates by sex and single year of age from the NCHS life
   tables, interpolated between the 1999–2001 table and the annual tables for
   2018–2023 (the 1999–2001 rates are used before 2000 and the 2023 rates
   after 2023).
2. Multiplied by the county's own mortality ratio for six broad bands, from
   CDPHE's public 2025 county reports: the county's 2025 deaths in the band
   divided by what statewide rates would give it, pulled toward 1 by adding ten
   deaths to both sides so that a band with few deaths cannot swing far.
3. Applied to the county's person-years and scaled so that each county-year
   matches its published death total.

Births are each county-year's published total, split by sex with the
conventional ratio of 105 boys to 100 girls. Deaths at age *x* in a year are split half to
the people who were already *x* when the year began and half to those who
turned *x* during it.

## Validation

```{r}
#| label: identity

# For the state, population at the start of a period summed over the groups
# is the whole population at the start, so the identity can be checked here.
identity <- five |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    pop_change = sum(pop_end) - sum(pop_start),
    births = sum(births),
    deaths = sum(deaths),
    netmig = sum(netmig),
    .by = period
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = pop_change - births + deaths - netmig)

v_25 <- validation |> dplyr::filter(period == "2020-2025", grouping == "broad")
v_short <- validation |> dplyr::filter(period == "2024-2025", grouping == "broad")
```

**The identity closes.** For every period, statewide population change less
births plus deaths equals net migration summed across ages (largest gap
`r scales::comma(max(abs(identity$gap)), accuracy = 0.1)` people, from
rounding). By county and year, net migration summed across ages equals SDO's
published net migration exactly from 1992 on. The two SDO tables disagree by
up to 858 people in a county in 1991, the first year after the 1990 census
base, and by rounding of 10–20 people in 2001–2020; those gaps land in net
migration and are left visible rather than forced away.

**Estimated deaths against recorded deaths.** Recorded deaths, scaled to the
same county totals, were run through the same calculation inside the State
Demography Office, and only summary statistics are published here. The two
versions agree on every county's total; they differ only in how deaths are
spread across ages.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation
#| tbl-cap: "Net migration from estimated deaths against recorded deaths, county by age-group cells"

validation |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    grouping = dplyr::if_else(grouping == "five", "Five-year groups", "Broad groups")
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    Period = period,
    Grouping = grouping,
    Cells = cells,
    `Median difference (people)` = median_abs_diff,
    `90th percentile (people)` = p90_abs_diff,
    `Median difference (per 1,000 a year)` = median_abs_rate_diff
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = tidyselect::where(is.numeric), decimals = 1) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = Cells, decimals = 0) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::pct(88))
```

For 2020–2025 in broad groups the median county-group differs by
`r v_25$median_abs_diff` people and 90% by under
`r round(v_25$p90_abs_diff)`; for a one-year span (2024–2025) the median is
`r v_short$median_abs_diff`. The largest differences are in the oldest groups
of large counties, and they are biggest in 1990–2000, because the county
mortality ratios come from 2025 and county mortality patterns then differed
more from today's.

## Statewide pattern, 2020–2025

```{r}
#| label: fig-state-age-profile
#| fig-cap: "Colorado net migration by age, 7/1/2020 to 7/1/2025"
#| fig-alt: !expr paste0("Horizontal diverging bar chart of Colorado net migration by five-year age group in 2025. Bars are modestly positive for children, largest for ages 25-29 at ", lbl_signed(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "25-29")), ", positive through 40-44, and negative from 45-49 through 80-84.")
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

state_now |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_group = forcats::fct_rev(age_group),
    sign_grp = factor(
      dplyr::if_else(netmig >= 0, "Net gain", "Net loss"),
      levels = c("Net loss", "Net gain")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = netmig, y = age_group, fill = sign_grp)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = lbl_signed(netmig),
      hjust = dplyr::if_else(netmig >= 0, -0.12, 1.12)
    ),
    size = 3.1,
    colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  scale_fill_sdo_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(style_positive = "plus"),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.20)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Colorado's net in-migration is concentrated among young adults",
    subtitle = "Net migration 2020-2025, by age in 2025",
    x = "Net migration",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = source_caption
  ) +
  theme_sdo() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-state-broad
#| tbl-cap: "Colorado net migration by broad age group, 2020-2025"

broad |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000", period == "2020-2025") |>
  dplyr::arrange(age_group) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Age in 2025` = as.character(age_group),
    `Population 2020` = pop_start,
    `Population 2025` = pop_end,
    Births = births,
    Deaths = deaths,
    `Net migration` = netmig,
    `Per 1,000 a year` = rate_per_1000
  ) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = c(`Population 2020`:`Net migration`), decimals = 0) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = `Per 1,000 a year`, decimals = 1) |>
  gt::tab_footnote("Population 2020 is the same people five years earlier; those born since have none.")
```

Colorado's migration is overwhelmingly a young-adult story. The people aged
25–29 in 2025 added `r scales::comma(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "25-29"))`
over the five years, more than half of the state's net migration of
`r scales::comma(sum(state_now$netmig))`, and the 30–34 and 20–24 groups added
another `r scales::comma(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "30-34"))` and
`r scales::comma(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "20-24"))`. From 45–49 to 80–84
every group is negative, with the steadiest losses in the pre-retirement and
early-retirement years.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-county-broad

broad |>

  dplyr::select(county, age_group, netmig) |>

  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = age_group, values_from = netmig) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Total = rowSums(dplyr::across(tidyselect::where(is.numeric)))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Total)) |>
  dplyr::rename(County = county) |>
  gt::gt() |>

```

Four recurring shapes show up across the state.

**University counties** gain heavily at 20–24 and give much of it back in the
next group. Boulder adds `r scales::comma(v5("Boulder", "2020-2025", "20-24"))`
at 20–24 and loses `r scales::comma(-v5("Boulder", "2020-2025", "25-29"))` at
25–29; Larimer adds `r scales::comma(v5("Larimer", "2020-2025", "20-24"))` and
loses `r scales::comma(-v5("Larimer", "2020-2025", "25-29"))`. The students
arrive, and most of them leave again on schedule.

**Denver** is the young-adult magnet in its purest form: a total of only
`r fmt_signed(total_of("Denver"))`, but
`r fmt_signed(v5("Denver", "2020-2025", "25-29"))` in the 25–29 group alone.
The reversal comes immediately after: 30–34 is roughly flat
(`r fmt_signed(v5("Denver", "2020-2025", "30-34"))`) and the two groups above
it lose `r scales::comma(-v5("Denver", "2020-2025", "35-39"))` and
`r scales::comma(-v5("Denver", "2020-2025", "40-44"))`. People arrive in Denver
in their twenties and leave from their mid-thirties onward.

**Suburban and exurban growth counties** — Weld
(`r fmt_signed(total_of("Weld"))`), Douglas
(`r fmt_signed(total_of("Douglas"))`), Adams
(`r fmt_signed(total_of("Adams"))`) — gain across most age groups, and are
where many of the families leaving Denver and Boulder are landing.

**Resort counties** — Eagle, Pitkin, Summit — are net negative overall and lose
people at most ages. Their one consistent gain is at 25–29
(`r fmt_signed(v5("Eagle", "2020-2025", "25-29"))`,
`r fmt_signed(v5("Pitkin", "2020-2025", "25-29"))` and
`r fmt_signed(v5("Summit", "2020-2025", "25-29"))`), far too small to offset
the losses elsewhere: a young workforce that does not stay.

## The longer history, 1990 to 2025

**1990 is the earliest start possible.** The SDO age-detailed population tables
begin in 1990; the components of change reach back to 1970, but without age
detail.

The periods are different lengths, so net migration is **annualised** and
expressed per 1,000 of the group's average population, where average population
is the person-years lived in the period divided by its length:

$$
\text{rate} = \frac{\text{net migration} / \text{years}}{\text{person-years} / \text{years}} \times 1000
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-period-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Annual net migration rate by age at end of period, Colorado"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of Colorado's annual net migration rate per 1,000 by age at the end of each of four periods. The 1990-2000 line is positive at every age. The 2000-2010 line is lower but positive almost everywhere. The 2010-2020 line rises again at young-adult ages and dips slightly negative above 70. The 2020-2025 line nearly matches the 1990s peak at 25-29 but is negative from 45-49 through 80-84."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

five |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000") |>
  ggplot(aes(age_group, rate_per_1000, colour = period, group = period)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_sdo_discrete() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(style_positive = "plus")) +
  labs(
    title = "Colorado once gained at every age; now mainly among young adults",
    subtitle = "Annual net migration per 1,000 people, by age at the end of each period",
    x = "Age at end of period",
    y = "Per 1,000 per year",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = source_caption
  ) +
  theme_sdo() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-period-broad
#| tbl-cap: "Colorado annual net migration per 1,000, broad age groups"

broad |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000") |>
  dplyr::select(period, `Age at end` = age_group, rate_per_1000) |>
  dplyr::arrange(`Age at end`) |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Age at end` = as.character(`Age at end`)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = rate_per_1000) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = -`Age at end`, decimals = 1, force_sign = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: history-values

annual_by_period <- five |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000") |>
  dplyr::summarise(annual = sum(netmig_annual), .by = period)

annual_of <- function(p) {
  annual_by_period |> dplyr::filter(period == p) |> dplyr::pull(annual)
}

state_1990s <- five |> dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000", period == "1990-2000")
weakest_1990s <- state_1990s |> dplyr::slice_min(rate_per_1000)
negative_now <- state_now |> dplyr::filter(netmig < 0)
```

Statewide net migration ran at about
`r scales::comma(annual_of("1990-2000"), accuracy = 100)` a year in the 1990s,
`r scales::comma(annual_of("2000-2010"), accuracy = 100)` in the 2000s,
`r scales::comma(annual_of("2010-2020"), accuracy = 100)` in the 2010s and
`r scales::comma(annual_of("2020-2025"), accuracy = 100)` since 2020. The totals
swing with the economy; the age profile tells a slower and more one-directional
story.

In 1990–2000 Colorado gained people at **every age**. The weakest group,
`r weakest_1990s$age_group`, still ran at
`r fmt_signed(weakest_1990s$rate_per_1000, 1)` per 1,000 a year. Nothing since
has repeated it. The 25–29 rate went from
`r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "1990-2000", "25-29", "rate_per_1000"), 1)` in the
1990s to `r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "2000-2010", "25-29", "rate_per_1000"), 1)`,
`r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "2010-2020", "25-29", "rate_per_1000"), 1)` and
`r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "25-29", "rate_per_1000"), 1)`, while
in 2020–2025 every group from `r dplyr::first(as.character(negative_now$age_group))`
to `r dplyr::last(as.character(negative_now$age_group[negative_now$age_group != "85+"]))`
is negative. Colorado draws people in their twenties about as strongly as in
the boom, and no longer draws the families, midlife movers and retirees who
used to come alongside them. The 10–14 rate falling from
`r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "1990-2000", "10-14", "rate_per_1000"), 1)` to
`r fmt_signed(v5("Colorado", "2020-2025", "10-14", "rate_per_1000"), 1)` is the
same fact seen from the other end: those are the children of the families that
are no longer arriving.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Explore this by county
The [dashboard](dashboard.qmd) compares any county against others within a
period, or across all four periods, in five-year or broad groups, and forms
any span inside 2020–2025.
:::

A limit worth naming: a group ending a period at a given age lived through a
different stretch of its own life in a five-year period than in a ten-year
one. Annualising handles the length, not which ages were lived through, so the
comparison is sound in direction and broadly in magnitude rather than exact at
a single age.

### SDO's existing published figures

```{r}
#| label: sdo-published

sdo_published <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("output", "sdo-published-netmig-by-age.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
published_1020 <- sdo_published |>
  dplyr::filter(fips == 0) |>
  dplyr::summarise(netmig = sum(netmig1020)) |>
  dplyr::pull(netmig)
here_1020 <- five |>
  dplyr::filter(countyfips == "08000", period == "2010-2020") |>
  dplyr::summarise(netmig = sum(netmig)) |>
  dplyr::pull(netmig)
```

The office already publishes net migration by age for 1995–2000, 2000–2010 and
2010–2020 in `data.netmigrbyage`, written out here as
`output/sdo-published-netmig-by-age.csv`. It is **not** used as a control. Its
2010–2020 age detail sums to `r scales::comma(published_1020)` statewide,
against `r scales::comma(here_1020)` here, which matches the office's own
components of change; its level and rate columns also contradict each other
above age 65. Someone who knows that table's vintage and definitions should
confirm what it represents before the two series are reconciled.

## Caveats

**This recovers the migration implied by the population estimates, not an
independent measurement.** The SDO estimates are themselves built from vital
records and administrative migration signals. What this analysis recovers is
the net migration by age those estimates imply; it inherits their assumptions
rather than testing them. Any error in the population estimates lands in net
migration, because that is the term being solved for, and matters most in
small counties.

**County deaths by age are estimated.** County totals are exact, but the
spread of deaths across ages comes from Colorado life tables and one year (2025) of
county mortality patterns; see Validation. Rio Grande has no 2025 report and
uses the statewide pattern.

**Broomfield, 1990–2000.** Broomfield County was formed in 2001 from parts of
Adams, Boulder, Jefferson and Weld. The population estimates record the
transfer of its territory in estimate year 2000 as migration, so the 1990–2000
figures for those five counties include it; affected rows carry a note in the
published file and on the dashboard.

**The oldest group is the least reliable.** The 85+ group at the end of a
period is drawn from an open-ended group with very high mortality, so what
remains is small and its residual depends as much on the death estimates as on
anyone moving.

**Sex detail is noisier than the totals.** Births are split by a fixed sex
ratio, and the residual magnifies small differences in sex composition, so
individual cells by sex should not be read closely.

**Group quarters drive some of the sharpest patterns.** Prisons in Bent,
Crowley and Fremont and universities in Boulder and Larimer produce large
age-specific flows that are genuine population movement but institutional
rather than household migration.
